title: Aller, venir, partir, sortir
topic: present of aller, venir, partir, sortir; à and de with places; au, aux, du, des
why: Unit 3 opens with the verbs of movement: aller, venir, partir and sortir, the most frequent irregular verbs of everyday French. Along the way you learn the compulsory contractions au, aux, du, des and how to talk about cities, countries and transport.

{"lessons": ["

Aller and venir

Two of the most useful verbs in French are also two of the most irregular. Aller (to go) ends in -er, but it doesn't follow parler at all; venir (to come) has a stem that changes.

allervenir
jevaisviens
tuvasviens
il, elle, onvavient
nousallonsvenons
vousallezvenez
ils, ellesvontviennent
  • Aller mixes two stems: vais, vas, va, vont and allons, allez. Never “ils allent”.
  • Venir has the stem vien- when the ending is silent, but ven- for nous and vous. Ils viennent doubles the n, and you hear it.
  • Liaison with a z sound: nous‿allons, vous‿allez.

Aller also gives you the most common greeting: Comment ça va ? (How are you? How's it going?), answered with Ça va bien or simply Ça va.

— Salut Hugo ! Comment ça va ? — Ça va bien, merci !— Hi Hugo! How's it going? — I'm fine, thanks!
Je viens de Lyon, mais je vais à Paris ce soir.I come from Lyon, but I'm going to Paris tonight.

English often says “I'm going” with nothing after it. In French, aller needs a destination: Je vais au cinéma, Tu vas où ? And when someone calls you, “I'm coming!” is usually J'arrive !, not a form of venir.

", "

Partir, sortir, dormir

These three verbs share one pattern: in the singular they drop the consonant before the ending (partir → je pars), and in the plural they keep it (nous partons).

partirsortirdormir
jeparssorsdors
tuparssorsdors
il, elle, onpartsortdort
nouspartonssortonsdormons
vouspartezsortezdormez
ils, ellespartentsortentdorment

As with finir and attendre, your ear can tell the singular from the plural: in il part the t is silent, in ils partent you hear it.

Leave, go out, sleep

  • Partir = to leave, to set off: Le train part à huit heures. Je pars en vacances.
  • Sortir = to go out, to come out: Ce soir, on sort ! Careful: Il sort avec Léa means he's dating Léa!
  • Dormir = to sleep: Les enfants dorment.
Le samedi soir, nous sortons, et le dimanche, nous dormons tard !On Saturday nights we go out, and on Sundays we sleep late!

English “to leave” covers several French verbs. Partir means to set off, with no object: Je pars ! To say which place you're leaving, add de: Je pars de Lyon à midi. Never “je pars Lyon”.

", "

À, de and places

Aller goes with à (to, at), venir with de (from). When à and de meet le or les, they merge into a single word. These contractions are compulsory.

àde
+ leau cinémadu cinéma
+ laà la garede la gare
+ l'à l'aéroportde l'aéroport
+ lesaux États-Unisdes États-Unis

Cities and countries

Cities take à and de with no article: Je vais à Paris, Je viens de Lyon. For countries, it depends on the gender. Most countries ending in -e are feminine: they take en (to, in) and de (from). Masculine countries take au and du, plural ones aux and des.

Countryto / infrom
la Franceen Francede France
l'Italieen Italied'Italie
le Japonau Japondu Japon
le Canadaau Canadadu Canada
les États-Unisaux États-Unisdes États-Unis

One exception to remember: le Mexique ends in -e but is masculine, so au Mexique.

Getting there

Transport you get into takes en: en train, en voiture, en bus, en avion, en métro. When you're on it, or on your own feet, it's à: à pied, à vélo.

Inès vient d'Italie. Elle va au travail à pied.Inès comes from Italy. She walks to work.

Think of au and aux as single words: never “à le” or “à les”. English speakers often write “à le cinéma” or “de les États-Unis”: French doesn't allow it.
